title: ⭐⭐ Practice: how much, how many at once, and which comparisons are figures

questions.prompt: Hedi's class walked up to the olive grove above Gafsa to plant young trees. They pushed the loaded cart over the old wooden footbridge, and the footbridge held. Complete the note Hedi wrote that evening: "The footbridge was ___ for the loaded cart to cross."

options.text: strong enough
weak enough
too weak
enough strong

questions.explanation: "strong enough" is the answer: adjective + enough + to says that nothing stood in the way, and here the cart did cross. It is also the quality the crossing needed, since a footbridge carries a load when it has strength, not when it lacks it. "weak enough" is correctly built and then names the wrong quality: you say that an old wall is weak enough to be pulled down, never that a bridge is weak enough for a loaded cart to go over it. "too weak" reports the opposite of what happened: too + adjective + to always means the action did NOT take place, so the cart would have stayed on the near bank. And "enough strong" puts the word in the wrong place: of the four adverbs of degree, enough is the only one that follows the adjective instead of standing before it.

questions.prompt: A school magazine has sent this line to the printer: "The last two birds of the species died in the island reserve in 1962, and the species is now endangered." The sub-editor stops the page, because one word makes the sentence untrue. Which correction does she make?

options.text: Replace "species" with "wildlife".
Replace "endangered" with "in danger".
Replace "died" with "drowned".
Replace "endangered" with "extinct".

questions.explanation: "Replace \"endangered\" with \"extinct\"." is the correction. The line says the last two birds died, so no living member is left anywhere, and that is exactly what extinct means. Endangered means at risk of disappearing, which supposes there are still animals alive to save. "Replace \"endangered\" with \"in danger\"." changes the words without changing the meaning, so the sentence stays just as untrue. "Replace \"species\" with \"wildlife\"." swaps a countable word for a collective one: wildlife names the wild animals and birds of a place taken together, and cannot name one single kind of bird. And "Replace \"died\" with \"drowned\"." invents a cause of death the line never gives, and leaves the false word untouched.

questions.prompt: Nizar is closing his talk on the new dam. He has two facts: the dam holds the winter water, and it supplies the town with electricity. He wants the second fact announced before he says it, so that his audience is already waiting for it when it comes. Which closing line does that, and is correctly built?

options.text: The dam holds the winter water, and it supplies the town with electricity.
The dam not only holds the winter water but also supplies the town with electricity.
The dam holds the winter water; it supplies the town with electricity too.
The dam holds not only the winter water but also supplies the town with electricity.

questions.explanation: "The dam not only holds the winter water but also supplies the town with electricity." is the line: not only warns the audience that a second fact is on its way before it arrives, and but also delivers it, which is the announcement Nizar is after. Both members here are verb phrases, holds the winter water and supplies the town with electricity, so the two sides are of the same grammatical kind and the line is correctly built. "The dam holds the winter water, and it supplies the town with electricity." is correct English, but plain and announces nothing: it lines the two facts up and lets the second one arrive unheralded. "The dam holds the winter water; it supplies the town with electricity too." is correct as well, and does even less: too at the end of a sentence marks the second fact as an afterthought, once it has already been said. And "The dam holds not only the winter water but also supplies the town with electricity." does announce something, but it is broken: not only has been placed after the verb, so the first member is a noun phrase and the second a verb phrase, and the law of the structure is that the two members must be of the same kind.

questions.prompt: A pupil in Nabeul has written this line in her paragraph on the two dams of the valley: "The new dam is as high as the old one." Her neighbour reads it over her shoulder and tells her she has just written a simile. What is that line really?

options.text: A simile: the sign as ... as is there, and that is what a simile needs.
A metaphor: the line says that one dam is in fact the other one.
An ordinary comparison: two dams are things of the same kind.
A personification: the line lends a human quality to a thing.

questions.explanation: "An ordinary comparison: two dams are things of the same kind." is the true answer. A figure of style holds together two things of DIFFERENT kinds, a dry field and a sheet of paper, a river and a road; here one dam is measured against another dam, exactly as you would say that one pupil is as tall as another, and nothing is being pictured as anything else. "A simile: the sign as ... as is there, and that is what a simile needs." is her neighbour's mistake: the sign is the second step of the test and never the first, and between two things of the same kind as ... as only measures. "A metaphor: the line says that one dam is in fact the other one." reads a sentence that is not on the page: the line says the two dams are of the same height, not that they are one and the same dam. And "A personification: the line lends a human quality to a thing." names the third figure your book offers, the one that gives a human act or feeling to a thing, and nothing in the line does that.

questions.prompt: Two pupils describe the same dry river bed for the school magazine. Wassim writes: "By August the river bed was as white as a page." Mouna writes: "By August the river bed was a white page." Which statement about the two sentences is true?

options.text: Wassim wrote a simile, Mouna wrote a metaphor.
Wassim wrote a metaphor, Mouna wrote a simile.
Both wrote similes, because both compare the river bed to a page.
Both wrote metaphors, because neither of them uses the word like.

questions.explanation: "Wassim wrote a simile, Mouna wrote a metaphor." is true. A simile announces its comparison with a sign, like or as ... as, and Wassim uses as ... as. A metaphor makes the same comparison with no sign at all: Mouna does not say the river bed was like a page, she says it WAS one. "Wassim wrote a metaphor, Mouna wrote a simile." reverses the two, and gives the name metaphor to the sentence that carries the sign. "Both wrote similes, because both compare the river bed to a page." mistakes the definition: the two figures both compare, and what separates them is not the comparison but whether it is announced. And "Both wrote metaphors, because neither of them uses the word like." forgets that like is not the only sign of a simile: as ... as is the other, and Wassim uses it.

questions.prompt: A teacher writes this sentence on the board: "The tap of the water tank was too high for Skander to reach." She then asks the class which two plain facts she started from before she joined them into that one sentence. Which pair is it?

options.text: The tap was high. Skander reached it with difficulty.
The tap was not high enough. Skander did not reach it.
The tap was high. Skander had to reach it anyway.
The tap was very high. Skander did not reach it.

questions.explanation: "The tap was very high. Skander did not reach it." is the pair. Your grammar summary takes its own example apart in exactly this way: You are too young to understand, in brackets, you do not understand because you are too young. So too + adjective gives the first fact and the infinitive gives the second one, in the negative. "The tap was high. Skander reached it with difficulty." keeps the difficulty but lets the action happen, which is what the structure rules out. "The tap was not high enough. Skander did not reach it." reverses the first fact: not high enough would mean the tap was too low for him, and only the opposite adjective turns a too sentence into a not enough one, as in too high and not low enough. And "The tap was high. Skander had to reach it anyway." adds an obligation that appears nowhere in the sentence.
